fixes.explanation: The text gives the reason. The people “remained silent and did not answer a word, for Hezekiah had commanded…” them not to answer him. So their quiet wasn't an accident. Hezekiah, Judah's king, gave an order, and the wall followed it.

The verse gives the reason outright. The people “remained silent and did not answer a word, for Hezekiah had commanded…” them not to answer him. Hezekiah, Judah's king, told them ahead of time. So the silence came from his command.

Hezekiah hands over all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace. That's two places he's pulling silver from. It's like checking every coat pocket and couch cushion you own for change. Hezekiah, Judah's king, is trying to cover what Assyria demanded.

No ships pull into this story, friend. The silver is all that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace. Hezekiah, Judah's king, hands that over. If a cargo ship had shown up, it would have been a much easier day.

Right, and that's the sting of it. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh, along with a great army…” Hezekiah, Judah's king, had already sent his payment. Think of sending a payment and still having a collector show up at your door.

Not this time, friend. The text says, “Then they called for the king.” But the ones who went out to them were Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder. The king isn't on that list.

Egypt is the one he names. He says, “Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it.” He also names Pharaoh king of Egypt. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, has his claim ready, and it comes with a picture.

Moab isn't in this speech, friend. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “Look now, you are trusting in Egypt…” Then he brings Pharaoh king of Egypt into it too. Moab didn't even get invited to this one.

No price per horse gets named. The catch is in the last part of his offer: “…if you can put riders on them!” The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, attaches that challenge to the horses. The condition is about riders, not payment.

The LORD is the name he uses. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’…” That's what he claims. It's the boldest thing he's said so far.
He's not going anywhere, friend. The text says the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew. No walking back to camp happens in this verse. He stays put and keeps talking.
No letter in this scene. The Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew. He's talking out loud, and the people on the wall are in earshot. It's a shout, not a note.

He says the opposite. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, tells the people, “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand.” That's him telling the crowd on the wall not to count on Hezekiah, their king. It comes right after he calls them to hear the word of the king of Assyria.

That's what he says. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, speaks of the vine, the fig tree and the cistern, then says, “…until I come and take you away to a land like your own…” So the picture he paints has a move in it. It's a sales pitch with a move hidden inside.

He's not talking about keeping Hezekiah. In fact the Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, keeps telling them not to listen to Hezekiah. What he says is, “…until I come and take you away to a land like your own…” So what he describes is being taken away.

Samaria is the name he drops. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks, “Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?” It's a roll call, and Samaria is the last name on it. He's counting off places like a man reading a very long guest list.
Silence it is. The text says, “But the people remained silent and did not answer a word…” After all that shouting, nobody says a thing. I'd have at least cleared my throat, friend.
Gates don't come up in this passage, friend. The text says the people “…remained silent and did not answer a word…” That's their whole answer to him. Words are the thing they don't give.

They came to Hezekiah “…with their clothes torn…” That's Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder, the same three who went out to the Rabshakeh. The text doesn't say why their clothes were torn. I think the words they heard hit them hard.

Nothing about feet, friend. Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder came to Hezekiah “…with their clothes torn…” That's the detail the text hands us, so I'd skip the shoe check and look at the clothes. After that, they tell him what the Rabshakeh said.
